{{Short description|Exact floating-point subtraction theorem}}
In [[floating-point arithmetic]], the '''Sterbenz lemma''' or '''Sterbenz's lemma'''<ref name="handbook">{{cite book
|last1=Muller
|first1=Jean-Michel
|last2=Brunie
|first2=Nicolas
|last3=de Dinechin
|first3=Florent
|last4=Jeannerod
|first4=Claude-Pierre
|last5=Joldes
|first5=Mioara
|last6=Lefèvre
|first6=Vincent
|last7=Melquiond
|first7=Guillaume
|last8=Revol
|first8=Nathalie
|author8-link=Nathalie Revol
|last9=Torres
|first9=Serge
|title=Handbook of Floating-Point Arithmetic
|date=2018
|publisher=Birkhäuser
|location=Gewerbestrasse 11, 6330 Cham, Switzerland
|isbn=978-3-319-76525-9
|at=Lemma 4.1, p. 101
|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-76526-6
|edition=2nd
|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-76526-6
}}</ref> is a theorem giving conditions under which floating-point differences are computed exactly.
It is named after [[Pat Holmes Sterbenz]], who published a variant of it in 1974.<ref name="sterbenz">{{cite book
|last1=Sterbenz
|first1=Pat H.
|title=Floating-Point Computation
|date=1974
|publisher=Prentice-Hall
|location=Englewood Cliffs, NJ, United States
|isbn=0-13-322495-3
|at=Theorem 4.3.1 and Corollary, p. 138
|url=https://archive.org/details/SterbenzFloatingPointComputation/page/n153/mode/2up}}</ref>

{{math_theorem
|name=Sterbenz lemma
|math_statement=In a [[Floating-point arithmetic#Floating-point numbers|floating-point number system]] with [[subnormal numbers]], if <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are floating-point numbers such that

<math display="block">\frac{y}{2} \leq x \leq 2 y,</math>

then <math>x - y</math> is also a floating-point number.
Thus, a correctly rounded floating-point subtraction

<math display="block">x \ominus y = \operatorname{fl}(x - y) = x - y</math>

is computed exactly.
}}

The Sterbenz lemma applies to [[IEEE 754]], the most widely used floating-point number system in computers.

== Proof ==
Let <math>\beta</math> be the radix of the floating-point system and <math>p</math> the precision.

Consider several easy cases first:

* If <math>x</math> is zero then <math>x - y = -y</math>, and if <math>y</math> is zero then <math>x - y = x</math>, so the result is trivial because floating-point negation is always exact.

* If <math>x = y</math> the result is zero and thus exact.

* If <math>x < 0</math> then we must also have <math>y/2 \leq x < 0</math> so <math>y < 0</math>.  In this case, <math>x - y = -(-x - -y)</math>, so the result follows from the theorem restricted to <math>x, y \geq 0</math>.

* If <math>x \leq y</math>, we can write <math>x - y = -(y - x)</math> with <math>x/2 \leq y \leq 2 x</math>, so the result follows from the theorem restricted to <math>x \geq y</math>.

For the rest of the proof, assume <math>0 < y < x \leq 2 y</math> [[without loss of generality]].

Write <math>x, y > 0</math> in terms of their positive integral significands <math>s_x, s_y \leq \beta^p - 1</math> and minimal exponents <math>e_x, e_y</math>:

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
  x &= s_x \cdot \beta^{e_x - p + 1} \\
  y &= s_y \cdot \beta^{e_y - p + 1}
\end{align}
</math>

Note that <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> may be subnormal&mdash;we do not assume <math>s_x, s_y \geq \beta^{p - 1}</math>.

The subtraction gives:

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
  x - y
  &= s_x \cdot \beta^{e_x - p + 1}
     - s_y \cdot \beta^{e_y - p + 1} \\
  &= s_x \beta^{e_x - e_y} \cdot \beta^{e_y - p + 1}
     - s_y \cdot \beta^{e_y - p + 1} \\
  &= (s_x \beta^{e_x - e_y} - s_y) \cdot \beta^{e_y - p + 1}.
\end{align}
</math>

Let <math>s' = s_x \beta^{e_x - e_y} - s_y</math>.
Since <math>0 < y < x</math> we have:

* <math>e_y \leq e_x</math>, so <math>e_x - e_y \geq 0</math>, from which we can conclude <math>\beta^{e_x - e_y}</math> is an integer and therefore so is <math>s' = s_x \beta^{e_x - e_y} - s_y</math>; and
* <math>x - y > 0</math>, so <math>s' > 0</math>.

Further, since <math>x \leq 2 y</math>, we have <math>x - y \leq y</math>, so that

<math display="block">
  s' \cdot \beta^{e_y - p + 1} = x - y \leq y = s_y \cdot \beta^{e_y - p + 1}
</math>

which implies that

<math display="block">
  0 < s' \leq s_y \leq \beta^p - 1.
</math>

Hence

<math display="block">
  x - y = s' \cdot \beta^{e_y - p + 1},
  \quad \text{for} \quad
  0 < s' \leq \beta^p - 1,
</math>

so <math>x - y</math> is a floating-point number.
{{tombstone}}

Note: Even if <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are normal, ''i.e.'', <math>s_x, s_y \geq \beta^{p - 1}</math>, we cannot prove that <math>s' \geq \beta^{p - 1}</math> and therefore cannot prove that <math>x - y</math> is also normal.
For example, the difference of the two smallest positive normal floating-point numbers <math>x = (\beta^{p - 1} + 1) \cdot \beta^{e_{\mathrm{min}} - p + 1}</math> and <math>y = \beta^{p - 1} \cdot \beta^{e_{\mathrm{min}} - p + 1}</math> is <math>x - y = 1 \cdot \beta^{e_{\mathrm{min}} - p + 1}</math> which is necessarily subnormal.
In floating-point number systems without [[subnormal numbers]], such as CPUs in nonstandard flush-to-zero mode instead of the standard gradual underflow, the Sterbenz lemma does not apply.

== Relation to catastrophic cancellation ==
The Sterbenz lemma may be contrasted with the phenomenon of [[catastrophic cancellation]]:
* The Sterbenz lemma asserts that if <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are sufficiently close floating-point numbers then their difference <math>x - y</math> is computed exactly by floating-point arithmetic <math>x \ominus y = \operatorname{fl}(x - y)</math>, with no rounding needed.
* The phenomenon of catastrophic cancellation is that if <math>\tilde x</math> and <math>\tilde y</math> are approximations to true numbers <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>&mdash;whether the approximations arise from prior rounding error or from series truncation or from physical uncertainty or anything else&mdash;the error of the difference <math>\tilde x - \tilde y</math> from the desired difference <math>x - y</math> is inversely proportional to <math>x - y</math>.  Thus, the closer <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are, the worse <math>\tilde x - \tilde y</math> may be as an approximation to <math>x - y</math>, even if the subtraction itself is computed exactly.
In other words, the Sterbenz lemma shows that subtracting nearby floating-point numbers is exact, but if the numbers one ''has'' are approximations then even their exact difference may be far off from the difference of numbers one ''wanted'' to subtract.

== Use in numerical analysis ==
The Sterbenz lemma is instrumental in proving theorems on error bounds in [[numerical analysis]] of floating-point algorithms.
For example, [[Heron's formula]]
<math display="block">A = \sqrt{s (s - a) (s - b) (s - c)}</math>
for the area of triangle with side lengths <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math>, where <math>s = (a + b + c)/2</math> is the semi-perimeter, may give poor accuracy for long narrow triangles if evaluated directly in floating-point arithmetic.
However, for <math>a \geq b \geq c</math>, the alternative formula
<math display="block">A = \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\bigl(a + (b + c)\bigr) \bigl(c - (a - b)\bigr) \bigl(c + (a - b)\bigr) \bigl(a + (b - c)\bigr)}</math>
can be proven, with the help of the Sterbenz lemma, to have low [[Error analysis (mathematics)|forward error]] for all inputs.<ref name="kahan-heron">{{cite web
